promptText: Why does JUnit 5 require @BeforeAll methods to be static by default, and what changes if the class is annotated @TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS)?
options: By default JUnit creates a new test instance per test method, so @BeforeAll must be static to run once across instances; PER_CLASS reuses a single instance, allowing @BeforeAll to be non-static, at the cost of needing to watch for state leaking between tests
@BeforeAll must always be static no matter which @TestInstance lifecycle is configured
PER_CLASS lifecycle disables @BeforeAll entirely and requires @BeforeEach instead
@TestInstance only affects parallel test execution and has no bearing on lifecycle annotations
explanation: JUnit 5's default per-method instance model is why @BeforeAll needs a static method; PER_CLASS trades that requirement away by reusing one instance, which is convenient but reintroduces the risk of leaking state across test methods.

promptText: What is the precise advantage of assertThrows over JUnit 4's @Test(expected = ...)?
options: assertThrows scopes the expectation to exactly the call under test - so a different line throwing the same exception type won't cause a false pass - and it returns the caught exception so you can also assert on its message
assertThrows runs measurably faster because it avoids reflection entirely
@Test(expected = ...) cannot be used with any checked exception subtype
assertThrows automatically retries the test if the exception's message text doesn't match exactly
explanation: @Test(expected=...) can't pinpoint which line threw or assert on the message; assertThrows wraps exactly the call you care about in a lambda, so an unrelated line throwing the same exception type won't produce a false pass.

promptText: Both stubs and mocks are "test doubles." What distinction does the chapter draw between them?
options: A stub returns canned answers to help the test proceed (state setup); a mock is a stub you also verify interactions on, asserting that a specific call - like emailService.send() - actually happened
A stub can only be created with Mockito, while a mock requires a hand-written class
A mock never returns any value at all, while a stub always must
There is no real difference; the chapter treats the two terms as fully interchangeable in every context
explanation: The chapter's key distinction: a stub feeds the test data so it can proceed, while a mock is used to assert that a particular interaction occurred - which is why over-using verify() couples a test to implementation details.

promptText: Why must you write doThrow(...).when(mock).voidMethod() instead of when(mock.voidMethod()).thenThrow(...) to stub an exception on a void method?
options: You cannot pass a void method call as an argument to when(), since when() expects an actual return value to stub against
doThrow() is simply a shorter alias for when().thenThrow() with no functional difference between them
Void methods cannot be mocked by Mockito under any syntax at all
when().thenThrow() only works for methods that return a primitive type, never for reference types
explanation: when(mock.voidMethod()) can't compile meaningfully because a void call has no return value to pass as when()'s argument; doThrow().when() sidesteps this by starting from the stubbing side instead.

promptText: Why does the chapter warn against defaulting to @SpringBootTest for a service-layer unit test?
options: Loading the full Spring context is the heaviest annotation available and can turn a 2-second test suite into a 5-minute one; a true unit test should construct the service directly (or via @InjectMocks) with mocked dependencies
@SpringBootTest cannot be combined with Mockito annotations under any configuration
@SpringBootTest has been deprecated and removed as of Spring Boot 3
Service layer classes physically cannot be instantiated without a live database connection
explanation: The chapter calls this the most common real-world mistake: sprinkling @SpringBootTest everywhere 'to be safe' turns a fast suite into a slow one, when a pure service-layer test should mock its collaborators and never load Spring at all.

promptText: Inside a @WebMvcTest slice test, what does @MockBean do that a plain Mockito @Mock field would not?
options: @MockBean replaces the actual bean inside the (partial) Spring application context that @WebMvcTest still loads, which MockMvc then runs against - a plain @Mock has no relationship to that context
@MockBean is functionally identical to @Mock and exists purely for naming consistency with Spring's other annotations
@MockBean can only be used inside @DataJpaTest and is invalid inside @WebMvcTest
@MockBean disables all HTTP request mapping for the controller under test
explanation: @WebMvcTest still loads a slice of the Spring context to wire up MockMvc; @MockBean swaps a real bean for a mock inside that context, which is exactly what a controller test needs since it can't use a bare Mockito mock the container never sees.

promptText: What is the practical difference in scope between @WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest and @SpringBootTest, and why does that difference matter for test speed?
options: @WebMvcTest loads only the web layer (controllers/filters, with services mocked); @DataJpaTest loads only the JPA layer plus an in-memory database; @SpringBootTest loads the full application context - each is progressively heavier and suited to a narrower purpose
All three load an identical amount of the Spring context; they differ only in which annotations are legal on the test class
@DataJpaTest cannot be paired with an in-memory database under any circumstances and always requires a real one
@WebMvcTest is the single heaviest of the three because it must simulate a full servlet container end to end
explanation: Spring Boot's test slices exist precisely to load only the part of the context a given test needs, keeping tests fast and focused; reaching for @SpringBootTest by default defeats that purpose.

promptText: The chapter says 100% code coverage is not the goal. What is the actual gap coverage leaves, and which related metric does it recommend paying closer attention to?
options: Coverage measures which lines executed, not whether behavior was actually asserted, so you can hit 100% with tests that assert nothing; branch coverage is the more honest metric for logic-heavy code, since a single if can be 100% line-covered while only one branch is ever exercised
100% line coverage is only achievable with a mutation-testing tool, never with JUnit assertions alone
Line coverage is always a strictly more meaningful metric than branch coverage for any codebase
Coverage tooling is fundamentally incapable of measuring anything above roughly 80% accuracy
explanation: This is the chapter's core coverage point: a fully line-covered if-statement can still hide an untested branch, so branch coverage is the more honest signal, and coverage overall is a tool to find gaps, not a target to chase.

promptText: A team's CI pipeline has started requiring engineers to re-run failing tests "just to be sure" before trusting a red build. According to the chapter, what is the correct response, and what are two of the most common root causes named?
options: Treat it as a bug (not a nuisance) and quarantine it so it stops blocking the pipeline while it gets fixed; the most common causes are real system-clock/date calls instead of an injected Clock, and shared or order-dependent state between tests
Delete the flaky test immediately, since any test that sometimes fails provides zero engineering value
Increase the test's timeout value repeatedly until it happens to pass consistently in CI
Flaky tests are an unavoidable property of JUnit 5 itself and cannot be meaningfully fixed
explanation: Silently re-running until green is exactly how teams end up ignoring real failures; the chapter's fix is to quarantine (not delete) the test, track it, and fix the underlying cause - commonly time/dates, random data, or shared state.

promptText: Why does the chapter recommend Testcontainers with a real Postgres image over an in-memory H2 database for integration tests, despite H2 starting faster?
options: H2 does not support Postgres-specific SQL, types, or constraints, so tests can pass against H2 while the equivalent code fails against the real production database - Testcontainers gives production parity at the cost of needing Docker in CI
H2 cannot be used with Spring Boot 3 under any configuration
Testcontainers is a hard requirement of JUnit 5 for any class annotated @SpringBootTest
H2 and Postgres share an identical SQL dialect, so the only real difference is startup speed, not correctness
explanation: The chapter's key argument: H2 tests can pass while production breaks precisely because H2 doesn't fully mirror Postgres-specific behavior - Testcontainers trades a Docker dependency for genuine production parity.

promptText: What does mutation testing (e.g. PIT/Pitest) measure that line or branch coverage cannot?
options: It introduces small deliberate bugs ("mutants," such as flipping > to >=) and checks whether your existing tests actually fail as a result; a mutant that survives (tests still pass) reveals a test that exercises the code but doesn't actually assert on its behavior
It measures exactly how many lines of code executed during a test run, which is identical to what line coverage already reports
It only detects performance regressions in the test suite's execution time, not correctness gaps
It requires rewriting every test to use a completely different assertion library before it can run
explanation: Mutation testing directly answers the '100% coverage but is it meaningful?' question: it catches hollow tests that run code without ever really checking its outcome, which coverage tools alone cannot detect.

promptText: Why is Thread.sleep considered an anti-pattern for testing asynchronous or scheduled code, and what does the chapter recommend instead?
options: Thread.sleep hard-codes a fixed wait, making tests both slow (always waiting the worst case) and flaky (failing if the async work legitimately takes longer); Awaitility's polling with a timeout, plus injecting a Clock for time-based logic, gives a deterministic and faster alternative
Thread.sleep is disallowed by the Java Memory Model from being called inside any class annotated @Test
Awaitility fully replaces JUnit as a test runner and cannot be used alongside it in the same project
Thread.sleep only causes flakiness under JUnit 4 and is perfectly safe when used with JUnit 5
explanation: The chapter names time and threading as the two biggest sources of flakiness; Awaitility polls for the expected condition instead of guessing a fixed sleep duration, and an injected Clock makes time-based logic deterministic.

promptText: A test class uses @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class), which enables strict stubbing by default. A developer stubs when(gateway.charge(100)).thenReturn(true), but the code path actually under test only ever calls gateway.charge(50). What happens, and what does it signal?
options: The test fails because strict stubbing detects a stub that was never used ("unnecessary stubbing"), which is a valuable signal that the test's setup is doing more than its actual assertions require
Mockito silently ignores the unused stub with no effect whatsoever on the test's outcome
The mismatch throws a NullPointerException instead of any Mockito-specific stubbing exception
Strict stubbing only applies to fields annotated @InjectMocks, never to fields annotated @Mock
explanation: MockitoExtension's strict stubbing fails the test on an unused stub precisely so it acts as a signal that the test is over-specified relative to what the code path under test actually exercises.

promptText: Using the chapter's testing-pyramid reasoning, why does inverting the pyramid (mostly slow end-to-end tests, few fast unit tests) hurt a codebase even when every test in the suite eventually passes?
options: E2E tests are slow and only tell you THAT something broke, not WHERE, so a mostly-E2E suite gives slow feedback and poor failure localization; the pyramid's large unit-test base exists specifically to give fast, precise signals, reserving E2E for a handful of critical user journeys
End-to-end tests are strictly more reliable than unit tests, so an inverted pyramid is actually the theoretically ideal shape to aim for
Unit tests are structurally incapable of catching regressions that end-to-end tests can catch, making the base of the pyramid mostly redundant
An inverted pyramid has no meaningful downside at all, provided the CI runtime budget can absorb the extra minutes
explanation: The chapter's phrasing is precise: unit tests tell you WHERE something broke, E2E tests tell you THAT something broke; leaning on mostly E2E tests produces a suite that is brittle, slow, and expensive to maintain, with weak failure localization.

promptText: Service A wants confidence that a breaking change to its API/schema won't silently break Service B in production, without running both services together in a slow end-to-end test on every commit. Which approach does the chapter recommend, and how does it work mechanically?
options: Consumer-driven contract testing (e.g. Spring Cloud Contract/Pact): the consumer's expectations are captured as a contract, and the provider's own CI generates and runs tests from that contract, so a breaking change fails the provider's build immediately without needing the whole system running together
Increasing unit test coverage on Service A's codebase alone is sufficient to catch this entire class of bug
Running a mutation-testing tool against Service B's codebase will automatically detect any incompatible upstream schema change
This kind of cross-service breakage can only be caught manually by QA after each deployment to a shared staging environment
explanation: Contract testing solves exactly the microservices problem of silently breaking a downstream service; it is far faster and more reliable than spinning up the whole system, since the provider's CI verifies compliance against the consumer's declared expectations directly.
